title: Why YOU Shouldn't Correct Wrong Answers
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin challenges the assumption that teachers are obligated to correct every wrong answer on every assignment for every student, arguing the practice is time-consuming, stressful, and ultimately ineffective because corrections imposed by the teacher don't stick -- students rarely even look at returned corrected work. His diagnosis is that when students have no personal stake in fixing their own mistakes, the correction becomes meaningless to them; the fix is to shift the responsibility for checking, questioning, and correcting work back onto students themselves. He acknowledges the natural objection ('won't students just sit there?') and answers that this only happens if the classroom culture of responsibility hasn't been established, which itself requires detailed upfront teaching. The piece supplies a small script of prompting questions ('How did you arrive at your answer?', 'Redo the problem and prove it') meant to push ownership back onto students rather than the teacher doing the cognitive work for them, framing this shift as central to building genuine student motivation and ownership.
points: Correcting every student's wrong answer yourself is time-consuming and ineffective because corrections imposed from outside don't stick with students.
Shift the responsibility for identifying and fixing mistakes onto students themselves -- they check their own work and ask for clarification rather than receiving corrections passively.
Use direct prompting questions like 'How did you arrive at your answer?' and 'Redo the problem and prove it' instead of marking answers wrong for them.
The 'won't they just sit there' objection only holds if the classroom's culture of responsibility hasn't been built through prior detailed teaching.
quotes: The culture of teaching demands that you correct every wrong answer for every student for every assignment AND ensure they understand what they did wrong.
Furthermore, and most critically, because it comes from you and thus is forced upon them, it doesn’t stick . They don’t learn from their wrong answers.
Stop doing it. No, this doesn’t mean that you won’t provide answers. But the corrections and thinking through mistakes must come from them. Otherwise, you’re just wasting time.

The more weight on their shoulders, the more purpose and motivation they have and the better they do. Therefore, the more you’re able to give them, defined by how well you prepare them, the more they’ll eagerly take on.
Otherwise, they won’t pay attention to your lessons. They won’t take responsibility for their learning. They won’t develop grit or ownership or want-to.
Setting students up for success with great lessons is your responsibility. Doing the work, which includes correcting, dissecting, and learning from their mistakes, is theirs.
